skill.name: benchmark-kernel
skill.description: Guide for benchmarking FlashInfer kernels with CUPTI timing and CUDA event fallback.
skill.summary: Benchmark FlashInfer GPU kernels with CUPTI or CUDA event timing.
skill.author: flashinfer-ai

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by Markdown inline code and fenced examples, not executable Ruby backticks. One high severity risk is confirmed: the tutorial recommends sudo nvidia-smi for locking GPU clocks, which changes host GPU state with elevated privileges. No prompt injection, data exfiltration intent, or network reconnaissance evidence was found.

remediation.suggestion: Remove the sudo example, or mark it as optional admin-only guidance that requires explicit user approval and rollback instructions.
State that shell examples are user-adapted benchmark commands and should not be executed automatically by an agent.
Recommend verifying CUDA compatibility and package source before installing cupti-python in shared environments.

content.value_statement: GPU kernel benchmarks can be inconsistent without clear timing methods. This skill guides FlashInfer users through CUPTI, CUDA events, backend comparisons, and CSV result capture.
actual_capabilities: Explains CUPTI timing and CUDA event fallback for FlashInfer benchmarks.
Shows benchmark workflows for attention, FP8 GEMM, and MOE routines.
Describes flags for iterations, warmups, reference checks, and CSV output.
Guides custom Python benchmarking with the bench_gpu_time helper.
Provides troubleshooting for CUPTI setup, noisy results, mismatches, and backend support.
limitations: Requires an existing FlashInfer checkout with benchmark scripts.
Results depend on GPU model, CUDA version, drivers, and installed backends.
Some guidance uses shell commands and one privileged nvidia-smi example.
Does not automate benchmark execution or validate generated CSV files.

use_cases.title: Compare attention backends
use_cases.description: Plan FlashInfer decode or prefill tests across FA2, FA3, cuDNN, CUTLASS, and TensorRT-LLM backends.

use_cases.title: Validate kernel changes
use_cases.description: Use reference checks, warmups, and repeated iterations before judging GEMM or MOE kernel performance.

use_cases.title: Prepare reproducible results
use_cases.description: Create tagged benchmark runs that save metrics and reproducer details for later comparison.

prompt_templates.title: Run a basic benchmark

prompt_templates.scenario: Select CUPTI or CUDA events for local constraints.
prompt_templates.prompt: I have CUDA and FlashInfer installed. Help me decide whether to use CUPTI or CUDA events for kernel timing.

prompt_templates.title: Compare benchmark backends
prompt_templates.scenario: Build a backend comparison with correctness checks.
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a FlashInfer backend comparison for attention kernels. Include warmup settings, reference checks, and result interpretation.

prompt_templates.prompt: Create a reproducible FlashInfer benchmark suite for multiple shapes and backends. Include CSV fields and review steps.

output_examples.input: I need to compare FlashInfer decode attention backends on H100.
output: Compare FA2, tensor-core FA2, cuDNN, and TensorRT-LLM if each backend is available.
Review median time, standard deviation, TFLOPS, and bandwidth before choosing a backend.

output_examples.input: My benchmark results vary across runs.
output: Increase warmup and measurement iterations before changing kernels.
Check GPU clock behavior, background load, and backend support.
Use reference checking to separate correctness issues from timing noise.

output_examples.input: I want to benchmark a custom kernel wrapper.
output: Use bench_gpu_time with representative tensors on the CUDA device.
Prefer CUPTI when available and fall back to CUDA events when needed.
Calculate throughput only after confirming the operation count and tensor shapes.

best_practices: Run reference checks before comparing performance numbers.
Use enough warmup and measurement iterations for stable statistics.
Save benchmark results with shape, backend, dtype, and hardware context.
anti_patterns: Comparing backends without confirming they support the target GPU.
Treating a single timing run as a reliable performance conclusion.
Changing GPU clocks or system settings without administrator approval.

faq.question: Does this skill require CUPTI?
faq.answer: No. It recommends CUPTI for accuracy, but FlashInfer can fall back to CUDA event timing.

faq.question: Can it benchmark attention and GEMM routines?
faq.answer: Yes. The guide covers attention wrappers, FP8 GEMM routines, FP4 GEMM, and MOE examples.

faq.question: Does it run benchmarks automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and command examples that users can adapt and run manually.

faq.question: What outputs should I inspect?
faq.answer: Inspect median time, standard deviation, achieved TFLOPS, bandwidth, backend name, dtype, and input shape.

faq.question: How should I handle output mismatches?
faq.answer: Use reference checking, inspect numerical tolerance, and compare verbose tensor statistics before trusting performance results.

faq.question: Is the privileged GPU clock command required?
faq.answer: No. It is an advanced optional step and should only be used with explicit administrator approval.
